title: Ayat al-Kursi
hookLine: the verse of the Throne: Allah, the Living, the Sustainer, neither drowsiness nor sleep (2:255)

lines: A GUARD, A THIEF, THREE NIGHTS.
cards: Abu Hurayrah, a companion of the Prophet, was put in charge of the charity food; Bukhari tells the story. One night a man crept in and took handfuls.
Abu Hurayrah grabbed him, heard he was needy, with a family to feed, and let him go. The next night, the same man, the same story.
On the third night Abu Hurayrah held on, and the thief offered a trade: let me go and I'll teach you words that will protect you. When you lie down to sleep, recite the verse of the Throne.
Abu Hurayrah told the Prophet, who answered: he told you the truth, though he's a liar. Today, from beyond Juz' 'Amma, a verse Muslims carry to bed: Ayat al-Kursi.

teach.b: It's verse two hundred fifty-five of Surah al-Baqarah, the second surah. Pickthall: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal.
Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Al-Hayy, the Living, depending on nothing. Al-Qayyum, which Pickthall calls the Eternal: the one who stands by Himself and holds everything else up.
Four days ago An-Naba' called sleep a sign: we are made to stop, cut off, and come back. This verse says the one who holds everything up never does.
Not even sinah, the first heaviness of the eyelids before sleep, touches Him. To Him belongs everything in the heavens and the earth. No one intercedes with Him except by His permission.
He knows what is before people and what is behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Then the word that names the verse: kursi. In everyday Arabic, a chair.
Pickthall says throne; some commentators say footstool, and one early explanation said it stands for His knowledge. It extends over the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire Him.
In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asked a companion which verse in the Book of Allah is greatest. The answer he approved: this one.
The week in one picture: you held the self back, heard the great news, slept and woke, remembered the sorting, and through all of it, the verse says, the One who holds everything up does not sleep.

how: Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after the obligatory prayers, and when leaving home, seeking protection; it is widely learned by heart and often hangs in calligraphy in homes.

o: a prayer said while seated on a chair
the Throne verse: the Living who never sleeps
a short surah about God's royal court

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: who stands alone and holds all up

s: it's verse 255 of al-Baqarah, the second surah.
in the story, the thief was the one who taught Abu Hurayrah the verse
the Prophet said he told the truth, though a liar (Bukhari).
kursi has only one meaning among commentators
throne, footstool, and in one early explanation, His knowledge.

games.q: you've caught the same thief three nights running. he offers words for protection if you let him go. what does the Prophet say later?
o: he told you the truth, though he is a liar
you should have taken him to court
games.why: Bukhari records: the words were true, reciting Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime. the Prophet added that the visitor was a devil.

practice: Think of what you'll put down tonight when you sleep: the unanswered emails, the person you're worried about, the thing that isn't fixed.

Set each one down, one per breath; you're allowed to stop, and the verse says the one who holds it all doesn't. If you pray, you can recite Ayat al-Kursi tonight as you lie down, as the night watch story suggests.
